SpO2 changes late, cuff pressure alone does not confirm position, and suction must stay available.

questions.stem: After prone positioning, SpO2 falls and peak pressure rises. What is the first action?
options: Increase FiO2 and continue the case
Deepen the volatile agent to reduce airway reactivity
Recheck airway position and circuit integrity
questions.explanation: Falling SpO2 with rising peak pressure right after prone positioning suggests the tube has kinked, migrated into a mainstem, or been partly dislodged, so the airway and circuit are checked first. Increasing FiO2, deepening anesthesia, or giving paralytic may help later but do not fix a displaced tube.

questions.stem: During otherwise stable maintenance, SpO2 abruptly falls from 99% to 88%. Which immediate approach best balances patient rescue with rapid equipment troubleshooting?
options: Raise FiO2, assess the patient, and check equipment
Assume monitor failure until proven otherwise
Replace the probe before assessing ventilation
Ignore it until a second monitor confirms it
questions.explanation: Unexpected desaturation requires immediate oxygen support with FiO2 1.0 while the patient, airway, ventilation, circuit, oxygen supply, and signal are checked in parallel. Assuming monitor failure or waiting for confirmation delays treatment of a potentially real hypoxemic event.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation, SpO2 remains 99% on FiO2 1.0 despite worsening V/Q mismatch. Which limitation of pulse oximetry is most relevant?
options: SpO2 directly measures the adequacy of ventilation
High FiO2 can mask worsening gas exchange
SpO2 directly measures the shunt fraction
A normal SpO2 excludes important V/Q mismatch
questions.explanation: On FiO2 1.0, enough oxygen is carried by blood from ventilated lung that SpO2 stays near 99% even as V/Q mismatch or shunt worsens during one-lung ventilation, until reserve is lost and saturation falls quickly. PaO2 trends and the A-a gradient reveal the deterioration earlier.

questions.stem: During a sustained recruitment maneuver at 30 cmH2O for 30 seconds, blood pressure falls from 110/70 to 75/45. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Vagal bradycardia from lung stretch receptors
Anaphylaxis to an agent given during induction
Less venous return from high intrathoracic pressure
Tension pneumothorax created by the maneuver
questions.explanation: Holding airway pressure at 30 cmH2O raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and right ventricular output, so blood pressure falls during the maneuver and recovers when pressure is released; hypovolemic patients are most affected. A pneumothorax would not resolve when the maneuver ends, and anaphylaxis brings bronchospasm and rash.

questions.stem: Which FOUR causes commonly belong on the differential for new intraoperative desaturation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: New intraoperative desaturation commonly comes from atelectasis, endobronchial intubation, pneumothorax, and bronchospasm, along with aspiration, pulmonary edema, and embolism. Light anesthesia and hypocapnia change heart rate and CO2 but do not themselves impair oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which event should prompt proactive reassessment of oxygenation and ventilation even before SpO2 changes?
options: Transfer to PACU after the tube is removed
Routine skin closure at the end of surgery
questions.explanation: Major position changes, insufflation, and the start of one-lung ventilation predictably change compliance, V/Q matching, and tube position, so oxygenation and ventilation are reassessed right away rather than waiting for SpO2 to fall. Skin closure and the end of preoxygenation do not carry the same risk.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, SpO2 falls to 92% and FiO2 is increased to 1.0, restoring SpO2 to 99%, but airway pressures remain high with dependent atelectasis. What does "treat the physiology, not the SpO2" imply?
options: Recruit the collapsed lung and add PEEP
Keep FiO2 at 1.0, since the saturation is normal
Replace the pulse oximeter probe and recheck
Deepen anesthesia to lower oxygen consumption
questions.explanation: Raising FiO2 to 1.0 hides the problem without fixing the dependent atelectasis that pneumoperitoneum causes, and high FiO2 can worsen absorption atelectasis. Recruitment and appropriate PEEP restore aerated lung and compliance, allowing FiO2 to come back down.

questions.stem: A breathing-circuit leak causes falling exhaled tidal volume shortly after induction. Which preventive check should have been completed before this anesthetic?
options: A machine check at the start of the week
A leak test before the case
A leak test once the patient is intubated
A leak test after a low-volume alarm
questions.explanation: A circuit leak test before every anesthetic finds loose connections, cracked tubing, or a faulty absorber seal before the patient depends on the circuit. A weekly check misses changes between cases, and testing after intubation or after an alarm means the leak is already affecting ventilation.

questions.stem: Which THREE broad domains are included in the ABCDE maintenance sweep? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The ABCDE maintenance sweep checks airway patency and security, breathing and ventilation, circulation, drugs and depth, and equipment and environment. Surgical progress, blood pressure, or neuromuscular blockade alone are single items within it, not domains.

questions.stem: During the "E" portion of an ABCDE sweep, which FOUR equipment checks belong there? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The E portion checks oxygen supply and the breathing circuit, absorbent and vaporizer level, pumps, alarms, and warming devices, and suction and emergency equipment. The surgeon's instrument count belongs to the surgical team, and music volume is part of distraction control rather than equipment safety.

questions.stem: Before a high-risk vascular dissection begins, the team confirms blood is immediately available; later, longer-acting analgesia is timed to expected closure rather than given reactively. Which maintenance skill links both decisions?
questions.explanation: Confirming blood before a high-risk dissection and timing longer-acting analgesia to closure both prepare for what is coming next rather than reacting once it happens, which is anticipation. Reassessment and documentation follow actions, and alarm response is reactive.

questions.stem: NIBP suddenly reads 68/34 mmHg, but pleth amplitude, ETCO2, HR, and the patient's appearance are unchanged. What should precede vasopressor treatment?
options: Give a large fluid bolus before checking the cuff
Give phenylephrine now, since any low NIBP is real
Confirm the reading and check other signs
Turn off every anesthetic agent immediately
questions.explanation: A sudden NIBP of 68/34 with unchanged pleth, ETCO2, heart rate, and appearance may be a measurement error from motion, a kinked cuff line, or arm position, so the reading is repeated or palpated and correlated with the rest of the circulation before treatment. If it is confirmed, treatment starts immediately.

questions.stem: Which THREE causes of intraoperative hypotension act primarily by reducing preload? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage removes circulating volume, and tension pneumothorax and high PEEP raise intrathoracic pressure and impede venous return, so all three reduce preload. Volatile agents lower contractility, nicardipine lowers afterload, and vagal bradycardia lowers heart rate; each causes hypotension through a different limb of the cardiac output equation.

questions.stem: HR and BP rise during knee arthroplasty. Before assuming light anesthesia, which THREE alternative causes should be considered? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Rising heart rate and blood pressure during knee arthroplasty may come from hypercarbia, a distended bladder, or tourniquet pain, which builds after about 45 to 60 minutes, rather than light anesthesia. Hypothermia, hypovolemia, and myocardial depression tend to lower blood pressure.

questions.stem: During propofol TIVA with paralysis, HR and BP rise abruptly and the infusion pump appears to be running. What should be verified before simply increasing the dose?
options: IV patency and actual drug delivery
questions.explanation: During TIVA with paralysis, a sudden rise in heart rate and blood pressure may mean the propofol is infiltrating or disconnected even though the pump runs, so IV patency and delivery are checked first. Analgesia and incision timing matter, but a delivery failure must be excluded before more drug is pushed through a failed line.

questions.stem: Persistent hypotension remains unexplained despite initial fluid and vasopressor therapy. Which escalation best improves continuous assessment and diagnostic precision?
options: Keep giving rescue boluses without reassessing
Add advanced monitoring such as an arterial line
questions.explanation: When hypotension persists despite fluids and pressors, intermittent cuff readings and empiric treatment are no longer enough, so an arterial line, and sometimes echocardiography, gives continuous pressure and helps find the cause. Changing vasopressors without new data does not improve diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which THREE elements belong in the surgical time-out immediately before incision? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The time-out happens just before incision and confirms identity, procedure, and site, prophylactic antibiotic timing, and the fire risk assessment, along with anticipated critical events. The final count belongs to the sign-out, the machine checkout is a pre-use anesthesia check, and the patient's own confirmation of consent occurs at sign-in while the patient is still awake.

questions.stem: During the time-out for a case with major hemorrhage risk, required blood availability cannot be confirmed. The surgeon asks to begin incision while the issue is checked. What does treating the time-out as a hard stop require?
options: Proceed if anesthesia documents the concern
Proceed if the surgeon accepts the risk
Resolve the required item before incision
questions.explanation: A hard stop means incision waits until every time-out item, including blood availability for a high-hemorrhage case, is confirmed. Documenting the concern or the surgeon accepting the risk does not resolve it, and completing the time-out after incision defeats its purpose.

questions.stem: During maintenance, which TWO findings most strongly support bronchospasm rather than reduced compliance? (Select 2)
options: Raised plateau with a normal peak-plateau gap
Reduced chest wall compliance on the loop
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm narrows the airways, so peak pressure rises with a widened peak-plateau gap, and expiration is prolonged with wheeze and a shark-fin capnogram. Reduced compliance raises plateau pressure with a normal gap and a square capnogram, and a larger tidal volume raises both pressures.

questions.stem: After intubation of an asthmatic patient, PIP rises to 40 cmH2O and the capnogram develops a shark-fin pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A peak pressure of 40 cmH2O with a shark-fin capnogram after intubating an asthmatic patient means slow, uneven expiratory emptying from bronchospasm, often triggered by the tube under light anesthesia. Esophageal intubation and disconnection lose the waveform, and malignant hyperthermia raises ETCO2 without this shape.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient is stable after intubation. Immediately after repositioning and intense surgical stimulation, PIP rises and a shark-fin capnogram appears. Which trigger is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm during maintenance in a reactive airway is most often triggered by intense surgical stimulation or airway manipulation when anesthesia is too light, so deepening anesthesia is part of treatment. Hypothermia, hypocarbia, and residual blockade do not trigger bronchospasm.

questions.stem: PIP rises to 42 cmH2O with diffuse wheeze and a shark-fin capnogram. Tube depth and circuit patency are acceptable. Which initial treatment best addresses likely bronchospasm?
options: Lighten anesthesia and reduce the FiO2
Give neostigmine to end the blockade
Give esmolol and keep the depth the same
Raise FiO2, deepen, and give albuterol
questions.explanation: Once tube and circuit problems are excluded, bronchospasm is treated by raising FiO2, deepening anesthesia with propofol or volatile agent, and giving an inhaled beta-2 agonist, with epinephrine if severe. Lightening anesthesia worsens reactivity, neostigmine increases bronchial secretions and tone, and esmolol can worsen bronchospasm.

questions.stem: If presumed bronchospasm does not improve, which FOUR mechanical causes should be excluded? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: When presumed bronchospasm does not respond, mechanical causes that mimic it must be ruled out: a kinked tube or circuit, a mucous plug, right mainstem intubation, and pneumothorax. Hypovolemia and light anesthesia do not create a mechanical obstruction.

questions.stem: Peak pressure jumps from 20 to 42 cmH2O and tidal volume falls abruptly. What should be checked first?
options: Replace the CO2 absorbent and recheck the pressures
Patient and airway: breath sounds, tube, kinks
Give a fluid bolus for low tidal volume
questions.explanation: A sudden jump in peak pressure from 20 to 42 cmH2O with a fall in tidal volume calls for checking the patient and airway first: breath sounds, tube position, kinks, biting, and secretions, often by passing a suction catheter. Treating it as bronchospasm or replacing absorbent before checking the tube can miss an obstruction that is quick to fix.

questions.stem: After trocar placement near the diaphragm, breath sounds disappear on the left and airway pressure rises. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Loss of left breath sounds with a sudden rise in airway pressure right after trocar placement near the diaphragm points to a left pneumothorax or capnothorax from pleural injury. Right mainstem intubation would silence the left side too but would not follow trocar placement, and esophageal intubation and bronchospasm do not cause one-sided silence.

questions.stem: With an LMA in place, high-pitched/croup-like airway sounds develop with rising resistance and poor ventilation. Which airway problem should be considered rather than assuming a simple device leak?
options: Normal function of a seated LMA
A Y-piece leak lowering airway pressure
questions.explanation: High-pitched, croup-like sounds with rising resistance and poor ventilation through an LMA suggest laryngospasm or bronchospasm, often from light anesthesia, so depth and airway reactivity are assessed and treated. A simple leak lowers airway pressure rather than raising resistance.

questions.stem: During spine fusion, which THREE findings support significant hemorrhage? (Select 3)
options: Increased pulse pressure or stroke volume variation
Saturated laps and blood in the canister
questions.explanation: Significant hemorrhage shows as hypotension with tachycardia, rising pulse pressure or stroke volume variation from falling preload, and visible blood in sponges, laps, and canisters. Rising ETCO2 with hyperthermia suggests a hypermetabolic state, bradycardia with hypertension suggests raised ICP, and a shark-fin capnogram suggests bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A hepatic vein is torn and blood loss becomes immediately massive. Which response best prioritizes the first resuscitative steps?
options: Give a vasopressor alone while awaiting labs
Call for help, O2, rapid blood and volume, monitoring
Deepen the volatile anesthetic to protect the heart
Treat the tachycardia with a beta-blocker first
questions.explanation: Massive hemorrhage calls for help, 100% oxygen, large-bore access, rapid blood product resuscitation with a massive transfusion protocol, vasopressors as a bridge, and an arterial line. A vasopressor alone does not replace lost volume, deeper anesthesia worsens hypotension, and the tachycardia is compensatory.

questions.stem: During spine surgery, BP drifts down and HR rises while the visible suction volume seems modest. Which action best addresses the possibility that blood loss is being underestimated?
options: Use ETCO2 by itself to estimate blood loss
Accept the surgeon's visual estimate as final
Check laps, canisters, drapes, and hidden blood
Wait for the hemoglobin to fall before acting
questions.explanation: Falling pressure and rising heart rate with modest suction volume suggest blood loss is being underestimated, so saturated laps and sponges, all canisters, drapes, and the floor are checked, and hemoglobin is measured. Hemoglobin lags behind acute loss, and visual estimates are often inaccurate.

questions.stem: A revision hip arthroplasty is expected to involve rapid major hemorrhage. Which vascular-access plan best supports high-flow resuscitation?
options: An intraosseous line as the planned sole access
A central venous catheter alone regardless of lumen size
Two large-bore peripheral IVs when feasible
questions.explanation: Flow through a catheter rises with the fourth power of the radius and falls with length, so two short large-bore peripheral IVs, such as 14 or 16 gauge, deliver blood faster than a long central catheter of similar gauge. A single 22-gauge IV is far too small, and intraosseous access is a rescue route rather than a plan.

questions.stem: Near closure after a long case, esophageal temperature is 35.4 ÃÂ°C despite stable hemodynamics. Which interpretation should drive active warming and emergence planning?
options: Above 35 C, the patient is normothermic
Temperature is normal until below 34 C
Core temperature below 36 C is hypothermia
questions.explanation: Perioperative hypothermia is a core temperature below 36 C, so 35.4 C calls for active warming and planning for its effects on coagulation, drug clearance, shivering, and emergence. Waiting until 35 or 34 C allows those effects to build.

questions.stem: A core temperature of 34.8 ÃÂ°C persists near the end of a long case. Which FOUR complications should be anticipated? (Select 4)
options: Bleeding from impaired platelets and clotting
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs platelets and clotting enzymes, increases wound infection, slows drug metabolism, and causes shivering that raises oxygen consumption. It prolongs rather than accelerates neuromuscular blockade and reduces hepatic clearance.

questions.stem: A patient's core temperature has fallen to 30 C. Which ECG finding is characteristic of this degree of hypothermia?
questions.explanation: Osborn or J waves, a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS and ST segment, are characteristic of moderate hypothermia below about 32 C, along with bradycardia and prolonged intervals, and the risk of ventricular fibrillation rises below about 28 C. Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia, delta waves preexcitation, and diffuse ST elevation pericarditis.

questions.stem: A patient remains hypothermic throughout a long operation and later develops a wound infection. Which mechanism plausibly contributes?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia triggers peripheral vasoconstriction, which lowers wound tissue oxygen tension, and it impairs neutrophil killing, both raising SSI risk. It does not speed bacterial clearance, warming does not contaminate wounds, and hypothermia does not reduce redosing needs.

questions.stem: How does a core temperature of 34 C change the volatile anesthetic requirement?
options: MAC rises, so more agent is needed
MAC falls, so less agent is needed
questions.explanation: MAC decreases by roughly 5% for each degree Celsius of hypothermia, so a patient at 34 C needs less volatile agent for the same depth, and the usual concentration can be excessive. Hyperthermia raises MAC. Hypothermia also slows clearance of IV drugs and neuromuscular blockers.

questions.stem: Near closure, core temperature is 35.2 ÃÂ°C despite otherwise appropriate anesthetic titration. Which emergence problem becomes more likely?
questions.explanation: At 35.2 C, slower hepatic metabolism, reduced Hofmann elimination, and lower MAC prolong sedatives, opioids, and blockers, so emergence is often delayed and active warming is needed. Hypothermia impairs platelets rather than helping, and shivering at emergence raises oxygen demand.

questions.stem: After induction, BP falls to 78/42 mmHg with a heart rate of 48/min in an otherwise healthy patient. Which vasopressor best fits this picture?
questions.explanation: Ephedrine has direct and indirect alpha and beta effects, so it raises blood pressure while increasing heart rate, which suits hypotension with bradycardia. Phenylephrine raises pressure through alpha-1 vasoconstriction but can cause reflex bradycardia, vasopressin is reserved for refractory vasodilation, and esmolol would worsen both problems.

questions.stem: During maintenance of anesthesia, a patient develops confirmed hypotension. End-tidal volatile concentration is 1.3 MAC and a large bolus of fentanyl was recently administered; heart rate is unchanged and there is no surgical blood loss. Which mechanism is most likely?
questions.explanation: High volatile anesthetic concentrations (1.3 MAC) combined with opioid administration lead to peripheral vasodilation, decreased sympathetic tone, and myocardial depression, resulting in hypotension. Tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, and hemorrhage present with distinct clinical signs (such as tachycardia, bronchospasm, or active surgical blood loss) which are absent here.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation with regular rhythm and appropriate tidal volumes, hemorrhage is accompanied by increasing pulse-pressure variation. What does this trend suggest?
options: A direct measure of hemoglobin concentration
Increasing myocardial contractility independent of preload
Preload dependence consistent with possible fluid responsiveness
questions.explanation: During controlled ventilation in sinus rhythm with adequate tidal volumes, pulse pressure variation rises as preload falls, showing that the heart is on the steep part of the Starling curve and stroke volume will likely rise with volume. It is not a measure of hemoglobin or contractility.

questions.stem: Ongoing vascular hemorrhage requires repeated blood gases/coagulation testing and beat-to-beat pressure assessment. Which monitor best serves both needs?
questions.explanation: An arterial catheter gives beat-to-beat pressure and an access point for repeated blood gases, hemoglobin, and coagulation tests during ongoing hemorrhage. A finger cuff gives continuous pressure but no blood samples, NIBP every minute still leaves gaps, and a central line samples venous rather than arterial blood.

questions.stem: Immediately after release of a prolonged lower-extremity tourniquet, BP falls without evidence of bleeding. Which mechanism best fits the timing?
questions.explanation: Releasing a long tourniquet returns acidic, vasodilating metabolites and allows reactive hyperemia in the limb, so blood pressure falls and ETCO2 rises transiently. The timing points to reperfusion rather than a vagal reflex or light anesthesia, which would raise pressure.

questions.stem: A hypothermic patient develops increased surgical bleeding and then vigorous postoperative shivering with myocardial ischemia. Which TWO effects of hypothermia help explain this? (Select 2)
options: Shivering-related increase in myocardial oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Hypothermia slows clotting enzymes and impairs platelet function, increasing bleeding, and postoperative shivering raises oxygen consumption and myocardial demand, which can provoke ischemia. Cold causes vasoconstriction rather than vasodilation, and it impairs rather than enhances platelets and enzymes.

questions.stem: Three otherwise similar patients receive equipotent volatile anesthetics for 3 hours. If rapid washout is now the priority, which agent's lower blood-gas solubility should favor the fastest emergence?
options: All three should wash out identically
questions.explanation: Washout depends heavily on blood-gas solubility. Desflurane has the lowest blood-gas partition coefficient of these agents, so it leaves the blood fastest when delivery stops. After a long case, the less soluble agent also accumulates less in tissue, which favors faster emergence.

questions.stem: A healthy middle-aged adult is stable under sevoflurane with an end-tidal concentration near 2%. Before considering age or adjuncts, this is approximately what anesthetic potency?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane's MAC in a middle-aged adult is about 2.0%, so an end-tidal concentration near 2% is about 1 MAC before adjusting for age or adjuncts such as opioids. Isoflurane's MAC is about 1.15% and desflurane's about 6%.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Why can nitrous oxide alone not provide surgical anesthesia at sea level?
options: It has no analgesic properties at all
Its MAC is above what can be delivered
It is too soluble to reach the brain quickly
It requires a heated vaporizer to deliver
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide's MAC is about 104%, which cannot be reached at atmospheric pressure while also giving enough oxygen, so it is used as an adjunct that adds roughly additively to a volatile agent. It does provide analgesia, it is poorly soluble with fast onset, and it is delivered from a flowmeter, not a vaporizer.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A patient receives 0.5 MAC of nitrous oxide together with 0.5 MAC of sevoflurane. Approximately what total anesthetic potency results?
questions.explanation: MAC values of inhaled agents are roughly additive, so 0.5 MAC of nitrous oxide plus 0.5 MAC of sevoflurane gives about 1 MAC, which is why adding nitrous oxide reduces the volatile agent needed. Opioids and benzodiazepines reduce MAC further.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: End-tidal desflurane is rapidly increased from about 6% toward 12%, followed by abrupt tachycardia and hypertension despite increasing anesthetic concentration. Which property explains the paradoxical response?
options: The higher level means lighter anesthesia
questions.explanation: Rapidly raising desflurane above about 1 MAC irritates airway receptors and triggers a transient sympathetic surge with tachycardia and hypertension, which can be blunted by raising the concentration slowly or giving an opioid. It is not lighter anesthesia, and desflurane has dose-related cardiovascular depression.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A child with reactive airways requires inhalation induction while spontaneous ventilation is maintained. Which volatile agent best combines nonpungency with bronchodilating properties?
options: Nitrous oxide as the sole anesthetic
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane is nonpungent, so it is tolerated by mask without coughing or breath-holding, and it is a bronchodilator, which suits a child with reactive airways. Desflurane and isoflurane are pungent and irritate the airway, and nitrous oxide alone cannot produce surgical anesthesia.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: After otherwise comparable 3-hour anesthetics, the isoflurane patient emerges more slowly than the sevoflurane patient. Which pharmacokinetic property best explains this?
options: Greater metabolism is the dominant cause
questions.explanation: Isoflurane has a higher blood-gas partition coefficient than sevoflurane, so more of it is held in blood and tissues and it leaves more slowly after a long case, delaying emergence. Potency and metabolism contribute little to washout.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A 30-year-old and an 80-year-old each receive end-tidal sevoflurane 2%. Which patient is more likely to be excessively anesthetized at that concentration?
options: The 30-year-old because MAC decreases in younger adults
The 80-year-old because MAC decreases with advancing age
Both equally because MAC is age-independent
Neither because 2% is exactly 1 MAC at every age
questions.explanation: MAC falls about 6% per decade after age 40, so for an 80-year-old, MAC of sevoflurane is about 1.5%, and 2% is roughly 1.3 MAC, which can cause hypotension and excess depth. The same 2% is about 1 MAC in a 30-year-old.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A stable desflurane anesthetic has reached equilibrium and no rapid concentration change is anticipated. Which fresh-gas flow meets low-flow quality targets while reducing waste?
questions.explanation: Low-flow anesthesia with desflurane and isoflurane uses fresh gas flows of 1 L/min or less once equilibrium is reached, which cuts agent waste and greenhouse emissions. Higher flows waste agent, and sevoflurane has separate minimum-flow labeling because of compound A.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During a stable low-flow sevoflurane anesthetic, the inspired concentration is increased but the end-tidal concentration changes slowly. Which principle explains the delay?
options: Low flow eliminates uptake into blood
The circuit is refreshed slowly at low flow
Sevoflurane cannot be used with low fresh-gas flow
End-tidal concentration is independent of delivered concentration
questions.explanation: At low fresh-gas flow, the circuit is less rapidly refreshed, so changes in vaporizer setting take longer to alter inspired and alveolar concentration. Temporary flow increases can speed wash-in or wash-out when a rapid change is needed.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which THREE benefits support low-flow volatile anesthesia? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Low-flow anesthesia rebreathes more exhaled gas, which lowers volatile consumption, cost, waste, and greenhouse emissions. The tradeoff is slower changes in circuit concentration and a greater need for gas monitoring, not faster depth changes or higher FiO2.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Sevoflurane is being delivered at low fresh-gas flow when sudden surgical stimulation requires a rapid increase in circuit concentration. Which adjustment accelerates the change?
options: Keep low flow and wait for slow equilibration
Turn the vaporizer off to reset the circuit
Raise fresh gas flow while adjusting the vaporizer
Reduce fresh gas flow further to concentrate it
questions.explanation: At low fresh gas flow, the circuit concentration changes slowly because little new gas enters, so temporarily raising fresh gas flow while turning up the vaporizer speeds the rise in inspired and alveolar concentration. Flow can be lowered again once the new level is reached.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which TWO situations particularly favor TIVA during maintenance? (Select 2)
options: Short outpatient case with no PONV history
Planned inhalation induction in a child
questions.explanation: TIVA is favored when evoked-potential monitoring requires minimal volatile agent and when PONV risk is high, as well as for malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. Inhalation induction, end-tidal agent monitoring, and volatile bronchodilation all depend on volatile agents, and short low-risk cases gain little from TIVA.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An older patient at high risk for postoperative delirium is being considered for propofol TIVA rather than volatile maintenance. Which statement best reflects the evidence?
options: Older adults clear propofol faster than volatiles
TIVA removes the need to avoid excess depth
Some studies suggest benefit; prevention is not assured
questions.explanation: Some comparative studies and meta-analyses have reported less postoperative delirium with propofol TIVA than volatile anesthesia, but findings are inconsistent, so TIVA should not be presented as reliably preventing delirium. Avoiding excessive depth and burst suppression still matters with any technique.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which THREE drugs are commonly used as components of TIVA? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: TIVA relies on IV agents such as propofol for hypnosis, remifentanil or other opioids for analgesia, and adjuncts such as dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and lidocaine. Desflurane, sevoflurane, and nitrous oxide are inhaled agents and are excluded by definition.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which FOUR setup steps are essential for safe TIVA during a long case? (Select 4)
options: Enough drug drawn up or available for the full case
The pump on emergency power with a charged battery
Infusion through a high dead-space carrier
Minimal dead space with visible connections
An IV site hidden under the drapes
questions.explanation: Safe TIVA needs enough drug for the whole case, pumps on emergency power with charged batteries, correct programming, and a short, visible line with minimal dead space. A high dead-space carrier delays and varies drug delivery, and a hidden IV can infiltrate unnoticed, risking awareness.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A propofol syringe empties during a paralyzed TIVA case, producing a gap in hypnotic delivery. Which planning failure most directly allowed this?
options: Too little drug and no ready backup plan
Use of an infusion pump for delivery
Use of more than one IV anesthetic
Use of processed EEG during the case
questions.explanation: TIVA needs enough drug prepared for the whole case and a backup plan, such as a volatile agent or a ready propofol bolus, so a syringe running out does not leave the patient without hypnosis while paralyzed. Pumps, multiple IV agents, and processed EEG are part of safe TIVA, not the failure.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During paralyzed TIVA, HR, BP, and processed-EEG index rise and inspection shows the propofol infusion is not reaching the patient. What is the immediate priority?
options: Restore hypnosis, then fix the line
Raise the rate through the same failed route
questions.explanation: Rising heart rate, blood pressure, and processed EEG with failed propofol delivery mean the paralyzed patient may be aware, so hypnosis is restored immediately with a bolus through a working IV or by turning on a volatile agent, and the failed line is fixed afterward. More paralytic hides the problem, and treating only the hypertension leaves the patient aware.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During TIVA with complete neuromuscular blockade, an infusion disconnects. Why may recognition of inadequate hypnosis be delayed compared with an unparalyzed patient?
options: Paralysis removes movement as an important warning sign
Neuromuscular blockers lower processed-EEG values independently of hypnosis in every case
questions.explanation: In an unparalyzed patient, movement is an early sign that anesthesia is too light, but complete neuromuscular blockade removes it, so a disconnected infusion may be detected only by tachycardia, hypertension, or a rising processed EEG, which are less reliable. Paralytics provide no amnesia.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During paralyzed TIVA, there is no end-tidal anesthetic-agent concentration to confirm hypnotic delivery. Which additional monitor can help assess hypnotic state?
questions.explanation: During TIVA there is no end-tidal agent concentration, so processed EEG gives the most direct information about hypnotic state, especially with paralysis. Train-of-four shows blockade, and heart rate, blood pressure, and pupil signs reflect sympathetic tone and opioid effect rather than hypnosis.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An older patient with dementia has a processed-EEG index of 32, but electrocautery produces abrupt spikes. How should the values be used?
options: Processed EEG is drug- and age-independent
Any value below 40 proves excessive depth
Interpret them with age, drugs, and artifact
questions.explanation: Processed EEG indices are lower at baseline in older patients and those with dementia, vary with drugs such as ketamine and dexmedetomidine, and are distorted by electrocautery and EMG artifact, so values are interpreted alongside the clinical picture and drug doses. A single value below 40 is not proof of excessive depth.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: During a long operation, repeated opioid boluses produce alternating oversedation and breakthrough sympathetic responses. What advantage can a carefully titrated infusion provide?
options: Steadier effect-site levels with fewer peaks
Higher peak concentrations with each dose
Faster emergence regardless of the opioid
questions.explanation: A titrated infusion keeps effect-site concentration more stable than repeated boluses, avoiding peaks that oversedate and troughs that allow breakthrough responses, often with a lower total dose. Accumulation can still occur with infusions of agents such as fentanyl, so emergence depends on the drug.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A remifentanil infusion must run at a very low rate where small delivery errors could meaningfully alter effect. Which device provides the most precise delivery?
questions.explanation: A syringe pump delivers small, steady volumes with high precision, which suits potent drugs such as remifentanil at low rates. Gravity drips and roller clamps vary with height, tubing, and resistance, so small errors can cause large dose swings. Manual boluses lose the steady-state control that the infusion provides.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An ERAS pathway reduces perioperative opioid exposure while maintaining analgesia. Which outcome pattern is most consistent with its intended short-term benefits?
options: Less opioid use and fewer side effects
questions.explanation: Multimodal opioid-sparing pathways aim to reduce perioperative opioid requirements and opioid-related effects such as nausea, ileus, and sedation, while supporting earlier mobilization and recovery. Higher PACU opioid needs, longer stays, and more ileus are the opposite of the intended outcomes.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Which FOUR nonopioid adjuncts fit an opioid-sparing plan for major abdominal surgery? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Opioid-sparing plans for major abdominal surgery combine NSAIDs, acetaminophen, magnesium, ketamine, lidocaine infusions, and regional blocks so each works on a different pain pathway. A morphine PCA or hydromorphone infusion relies on opioids rather than sparing them.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: A service wants to implement an opioid-sparing pathway across multiple surgical specialties. Which barrier is most realistic even if the pharmacologic rationale is sound?
options: Lack of evidence for multimodal care
questions.explanation: Opioid-sparing pathways depend on regional anesthesia skills, standardized order sets, and coordination across surgery, anesthesia, nursing, and pharmacy, which are common practical barriers. Nonopioid adjuncts do not raise PONV, PACU opioid use usually falls, and multimodal analgesia has strong evidence.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: An 82-year-old receiving dexmedetomidine is maintained on sevoflurane. Which THREE factors should be integrated when judging anesthetic depth? (Select 3)
options: Is the correct agent running with adequate supply?
Are inspired and end-tidal concentrations reviewed?
Is MAC adjusted for age and adjuncts?
Is the vaporizer set to 1 MAC regardless of patient?
Is the BIS turned off to reduce alarms?
Is the surgeon satisfied with the depth?
questions.explanation: Judging depth means confirming the correct agent is running with enough supply, reviewing inspired and end-tidal concentrations, and adjusting MAC for age and adjuncts such as dexmedetomidine, which lowers requirements. A fixed 1 MAC setting overdoses an 82-year-old, turning off processed EEG removes information, and surgeon satisfaction does not measure depth.
questions.topic: Volatiles, low flow, TIVA, depth, opioids, ERAS

questions.stem: Near extubation, facial-nerve monitoring shows strong recovery, but residual weakness remains a concern. Which quantitative monitoring site is preferred because recovery there better reflects residual peripheral blockade?
options: Posterior tibial nerve at the flexor hallucis
Facial nerve at the corrugator supercilii
Facial nerve at the orbicularis oculi
Ulnar nerve at the adductor pollicis
questions.explanation: The adductor pollicis, stimulated through the ulnar nerve, recovers more slowly than facial muscles, so a TOF ratio of 0.9 there gives the best assurance that upper airway and pharyngeal muscles have recovered. Facial muscles such as the orbicularis oculi recover early and overestimate readiness for extubation.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Both arms are tucked and inaccessible during surgery. Which site can be used to follow onset/depth of neuromuscular blockade until the adductor pollicis becomes available for recovery assessment?
options: The ulnar nerve under the tucked drapes
Facial nerve with a facial muscle response
questions.explanation: When the arms are tucked, the facial nerve at the corrugator supercilii can follow onset and depth because it resembles the more resistant laryngeal and diaphragm muscles, and the adductor pollicis is used for recovery when available. Stimulating under drapes is unreliable, and masseter or diaphragm assessment is not a standard monitoring site.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Train-of-four at the thumb shows 0 of 4 twitches, yet the patient develops hiccups and diaphragmatic movement. What best explains this?
options: The thumb is more resistant than the diaphragm
The nerve stimulator leads are reversed
The hiccups are a sign of light hypnosis only
The diaphragm needs more blocker than the thumb
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is relatively resistant to nondepolarizing blockers, needing roughly 1.5 to 2 times the dose that blocks the adductor pollicis, so it can contract while the thumb shows no twitches. Deep block, with a post-tetanic count, is needed to stop diaphragmatic movement. Lead reversal changes the response strength but not this pattern.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Nondepolarizing blockade is being maintained and intermittent redoses are planned. Which monitoring practice best limits unrecognized drift into excessive or inadequate blockade?
options: Rely on surgical movement rather than TOF
Check once after induction and at extubation
Check only when the surgeon reports poor relaxation
questions.explanation: Block depth drifts between doses, so quantitative monitoring at regular intervals and around redosing or reversal shows where the patient actually is. Waiting for movement or a surgeon's complaint means the block has already worn off, and infrequent checks risk a deep block at the end of the case.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient has partial neuromuscular recovery but requires another hour of surgical relaxation. Using a rocuronium maintenance redose of 0.1Ã¢ÂÂ0.2 mg/kg, which range is appropriate?
questions.explanation: A rocuronium maintenance dose of 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg for a 70-kg patient is 7 to 14 mg, guided by twitch monitoring. The range 42 to 84 mg is an intubating dose of 0.6 to 1.2 mg/kg, and 0.7 to 1.4 mg reflects a misplaced decimal.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: The surgeon reports abdominal movement despite apparent blockade. Which measurement should guide whether additional nondepolarizing blocker is actually needed?
options: Visual estimation of twitch fade alone
Quantitative monitoring with a numeric ratio
questions.explanation: Abdominal movement may come from light anesthesia, coughing, or returning neuromuscular function, so a quantitative monitor shows whether the block has actually receded before more blocker is given. Visual fade estimates are unreliable, a head lift cannot be tested under anesthesia, and surgical impressions alone lead to unnecessary deep block.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: TOF has recovered to 2 twitches, but fascial closure may begin within minutes. What should occur before another rocuronium dose?
options: Reverse the block before asking about timing
Clarify remaining surgical need and timing
questions.explanation: Two twitches may be enough relaxation for closure, and a redose minutes before the end risks a deep block at emergence, so the remaining surgical need and expected finish time are clarified first. Reversing before asking may leave the surgeon without needed relaxation, and monitoring continues through emergence.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Three patients are assessed before extubation: one has TOFR 0.65, one has TOFR 0.95, and one has two visible twitches. Which finding shows adequate neuromuscular recovery?
questions.explanation: A quantitative TOF ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis indicates adequate neuromuscular recovery, so 0.95 qualifies. A ratio of 0.65 is residual blockade, and two twitches mean substantial block remains.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Quantitative TOF shows T1 amplitude 20 mm and T4 amplitude 13 mm. Which interpretation is correct?
options: TOFR 0.35, so more rocuronium is needed
questions.explanation: TOF ratio = T4/T1 = 13/20 = 0.65, which is residual neuromuscular blockade because adequate recovery requires 0.9 or more. Further reversal or time is needed before extubation. Dividing T1 by T4 gives 1.54, and 0.65 is not adequate despite four twitches being present.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: During hip revision, hemoglobin falls to 6.8 g/dL. There is no unusual reason to avoid transfusion. Which action is most consistent with a restrictive transfusion strategy?
options: Give crystalloid, since Hgb does not matter
Consider red cell transfusion in context
Defer any consideration until arrival in PACU
questions.explanation: Restrictive strategies generally consider red cell transfusion when hemoglobin falls below about 7 g/dL, judged with ongoing blood loss, hemodynamics, and comorbidities, and a fall to 6.8 during hip revision meets that threshold. Crystalloid does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity, and waiting for 5 g/dL or PACU risks inadequate oxygen delivery.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Within 2 hours of a plasma transfusion, a patient develops hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, fever, and hypotension with a normal CVP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TRALI presents within 6 hours of transfusion, often after plasma-rich products, with hypoxemia, bilateral noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, fever, and hypotension, and a normal or low CVP. TACO causes hypertension, raised filling pressures, and responds to diuresis, while a hemolytic reaction brings hemoglobinuria and DIC, and a febrile reaction does not cause lung injury.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: After 2 L of crystalloid, MAP remains low and there are signs of developing pulmonary edema. What question is most important before giving another fluid bolus?
options: Has the patient produced urine this minute?
Has the surgeon asked for more fluid?
Can another liter go in before pressors?
Is the patient still fluid responsive?
questions.explanation: After 2 L with persistent hypotension and early pulmonary edema, more fluid helps only if the patient is still preload responsive, so responsiveness is assessed and other causes, such as vasodilation, myocardial depression, or obstruction, are considered. Reflex boluses risk worsening edema without raising pressure.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which TWO derangements should be anticipated during massive hemorrhage and transfusion? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Citrate in transfused blood binds ionized calcium, so rapid transfusion causes hypocalcemia, and cold products plus exposure cause hypothermia that worsens bleeding. Acidosis is typical early, with metabolic alkalosis appearing later as citrate is metabolized, and hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia is the main potassium risk.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: The surgeon estimates 300 mL blood loss, but the patient is tachycardic and multiple laps are saturated. Which approach best estimates true blood loss?
options: Combine all sources with vitals and labs
Accept the surgeon's estimate as definitive
Use suction canister volume by itself
Use a single hemoglobin value by itself
questions.explanation: Blood loss is estimated by combining suction volume minus irrigation, weighed or counted laps and sponges, blood on drapes and the floor, drains, hemodynamic trends, and serial hemoglobin. Any single source underestimates it, and tachycardia with saturated laps suggests more loss than 300 mL.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: A hemodynamically stable patient needs routine intraoperative volume replacement without hemorrhage or another indication for a specialized fluid. Which solution is the usual default?
questions.explanation: For routine volume replacement without hemorrhage or a special indication, a balanced crystalloid such as lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte is the usual choice because its electrolyte content is close to plasma. Hypertonic saline, D5W, and routine albumin are reserved for specific situations.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Urine output abruptly falls to 5 mL over an hour while MAP and other perfusion indicators remain stable. What should be checked first?
options: A fluid bolus before inspecting the system
Foley and tubing for kinks or obstruction
BIS as a measure of renal perfusion
A diagnosis of AKI from this urine value
questions.explanation: An abrupt drop in urine output while MAP and other perfusion signs are stable is most often a kinked, clamped, or displaced catheter, so the system is checked before attributing it to hypoperfusion or kidney injury. Fluid given for an obstructed catheter does not help.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which THREE scheduled therapies must be actively tracked during a long maintenance phase? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Cefazolin is redosed about every 4 hours, insulin requires timed glucose checks, and a TXA infusion follows a planned schedule, so missed or duplicated doses are a real risk. Urine output, end-tidal agent trends, and TOF counts are monitoring tasks rather than scheduled therapies, even though they are also checked regularly.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Diffuse oozing develops during massive transfusion. Which THREE laboratory approaches help guide ongoing hemostatic and blood-component resuscitation? (Select 3)
options: Conventional coagulation testing including fibrinogen when available
Viscoelastic testing such as TEG or ROTEM
Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit as part of overall red-cell loss assessment
questions.explanation: Conventional coagulation tests with fibrinogen and viscoelastic testing such as TEG or ROTEM guide hemostatic therapy, and serial hemoglobin helps assess red cell loss. D-dimer, bleeding time, and lactate reflect fibrinolysis, platelet function crudely, or perfusion but do not guide component dosing.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Ongoing surgical bleeding may use up the crossmatched units. Why should blood product readiness be reassessed during maintenance?
options: Type and screen expires after 1 hour
To avoid delay if more units are needed
Each unit needs a separate consent
questions.explanation: When ongoing bleeding may use up the crossmatched units, confirming with the blood bank that more compatible products are available prevents delay if hemorrhage accelerates. A type and screen remains valid for about 72 hours, and readiness rather than paperwork is the concern.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which THREE patient factors should influence opioid dosing during maintenance? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Opioid dosing during maintenance is adjusted for age and opioid tolerance, OSA and other respiratory risk, renal and hepatic function, and where the patient goes after surgery, since a monitored ICU bed tolerates more opioid than an outpatient discharge. Surgeon preference, room temperature, and planned depth are not patient factors.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: Which intravenous fluid, given in large volumes, most often causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of chloride, well above plasma, so large volumes raise chloride and lower the strong ion difference, producing a non-anion gap hyperchloremic acidosis. Balanced solutions such as lactated Ringer's and Plasma-Lyte contain less chloride and a buffer, and albumin is a colloid in a balanced or saline base.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: One patient has Hgb 7.5 g/dL with stable perfusion and no ongoing loss; another has Hgb 8.5 g/dL with active hemorrhage, MAP 55 mmHg, and worsening perfusion. Who has the stronger immediate transfusion indication?
options: The patient with the lower hemoglobin
Both, since each is below 9 g/dL
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin is only one part of the transfusion decision; active hemorrhage, instability, and worsening perfusion mean hemoglobin will keep falling and oxygen delivery is already inadequate. A stable patient at 7.5 g/dL without ongoing loss may not need transfusion under a restrictive strategy.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: After rapid administration of multiple citrated blood products, hypotension and ventricular ectopy develop. Which electrolyte abnormality should be checked promptly?
questions.explanation: Citrate in transfused blood binds ionized calcium. During rapid or massive transfusion, citrate delivery can exceed metabolism and produce hypocalcemia, which can impair contractility and vascular tone and contribute to hypotension and dysrhythmias.
questions.topic: Neuromuscular blockade, fluids, and time-dependent drugs

questions.stem: After anesthetic delivery is reduced, consciousness, spontaneous ventilation, airway control, cardiovascular regulation, and reflexes progressively return. Which concept best describes emergence?
options: A process that begins after arrival in PACU
Active pharmacologic reversal of every drug
A state that requires continued deep sedation
Gradual return of function as drug effect fades
questions.explanation: Emergence is largely passive: as anesthetic concentrations fall, consciousness, spontaneous ventilation, airway control, cardiovascular regulation, and protective reflexes return in sequence. Reversal agents address specific drugs such as neuromuscular blockers or opioids, and emergence begins in the OR, not in PACU.

questions.stem: Which THREE physiologic functions must return during successful emergence? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Successful emergence restores consciousness, the ability to keep the upper airway open, adequate spontaneous ventilation, and protective reflexes such as cough and swallow. Amnesia is not required, full cognitive recovery takes hours to days, and mild hypothermia does not by itself prevent emergence.

questions.stem: As anesthetic effect dissipates, ascending arousal pathways reactivate cortical consciousness. Which structure serves as a major relay for these arousal signals?
questions.explanation: Ascending arousal pathways from the brainstem and hypothalamus pass through the thalamus, which relays them to the cortex, so thalamocortical reactivation is central to the return of consciousness. The spinal cord, cerebellum, and hippocampus are not major arousal relays.

questions.stem: A researcher attempts pharmacologic stimulation of arousal during anesthetic unconsciousness. Activation of which receptor system has been associated experimentally with reversal of anesthetic unconsciousness?
questions.explanation: Experimental work has shown that stimulating nicotinic cholinergic receptors in arousal centers can reverse anesthetic unconsciousness, supporting the idea that emergence is an active neural process. Mu-opioid and GABA-A agonism deepen sedation, and neuromuscular nicotinic blockade affects muscle, not consciousness.

questions.stem: A patient remains unusually slow to regain wakefulness despite declining anesthetic concentration. Which pair of central structures is most directly involved in sleep-wake regulation and ascending arousal?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus and the brainstem reticular activating system regulate sleep and wakefulness and drive ascending arousal, so they are central to waking from anesthesia. The cerebellum and basal ganglia coordinate movement, the hippocampus and amygdala handle memory and emotion, and the sensory cortex processes input rather than arousal.

questions.stem: Sevoflurane is discontinued and fresh-gas flow is increased. What is the principal route by which the anesthetic leaves the body?
options: Hepatic metabolism of most of the administered dose
Pulmonary exhalation after redistribution from tissues
questions.explanation: Volatile agents leave mainly through the lungs: as fresh gas washes the circuit, alveolar concentration falls, and agent moves from tissues back into blood and out with exhalation. Sevoflurane is about 5% metabolized, renal excretion of unchanged agent is negligible, and there is no reversal agent.

questions.stem: Quantitative adductor-pollicis monitoring shows TOFR 0.85 after reversal. The patient otherwise appears strong. What should happen before extubation?
options: Ignore quantitative monitoring if head lift is sustained
Extubate because four visible twitches are sufficient
Extubate because TOFR above 0.7 excludes clinically important weakness
Continue recovery/reversal management and document TOFR at least 0.9
questions.explanation: A train-of-four ratio below 0.9 represents residual neuromuscular weakness even when the patient appears clinically strong. Quantitative recovery to at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis reduces the risk of impaired upper-airway function and postoperative respiratory complications.

questions.stem: A sufentanil infusion has been used throughout a long case, and timely spontaneous ventilation is wanted at emergence. When is it generally stopped?
questions.explanation: Sufentanil's context-sensitive half-time is short for infusions of a few hours but rises with longer use, so it is commonly stopped about 30 to 45 minutes before the end to allow spontaneous ventilation at emergence. Stopping 5 to 10 minutes before suits remifentanil, and stopping 2 hours early risks inadequate analgesia during surgery.

questions.stem: A remifentanil infusion is used for a case requiring rapid neurologic examination after extubation. Which plan best accounts for its rapid offset?
options: Stop it 30 to 45 minutes early with nothing else
Continue it unchanged into PACU transfer
Stop it near the end with longer analgesia on board
Stop it at induction to prevent accumulation
questions.explanation: Remifentanil wears off within minutes because of esterase metabolism, so it can run until about 5 to 10 minutes before the end, allowing a quick neurologic exam, but a longer-acting analgesic must be established beforehand to cover the pain that follows. Stopping it early without other analgesia leaves the patient in pain.

questions.stem: Other common causes of delayed emergence have been addressed, but repeated midazolam doses are still contributing to clinically significant sedation. Which specific reversal agent may be considered?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist that can reverse residual midazolam sedation once other causes of delayed emergence have been ruled out. It is titrated in small doses, and its shorter duration means resedation must be watched for. Naloxone reverses opioids, while sugammadex and neostigmine reverse neuromuscular blockade.

questions.stem: After surgery, clinically significant opioid-induced respiratory depression persists despite supportive measures. Which antagonist can be carefully titrated to reverse the opioid effect?
questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist, and small titrated doses such as 40 mcg reverse respiratory depression while preserving some analgesia. Large boluses can cause severe pain, hypertension, and pulmonary edema. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and atropine and sugammadex do not affect opioid receptors.

questions.stem: A long-acting opioid was given late in the case and the patient remains hypoventilatory as anesthetic depth decreases. Why does opioid timing matter during emergence?
options: Residual opioid can delay adequate breathing
Late opioid speeds emergence by analgesia
Opioid timing matters for nausea only
questions.explanation: A long-acting opioid given late in the case peaks as the volatile agent washes out, shifting the CO2 response curve and depressing ventilation, so spontaneous breathing may be inadequate at extubation. Opioids do not speed volatile elimination, and their timing affects ventilation as well as nausea.

questions.stem: A high-PONV-risk patient is approaching emergence. Which TWO strategies are most appropriate? (Select 2)
options: Minimize emetogenic anesthetic/opioid exposure when clinically feasible
Delay all prophylaxis until vomiting occurs
Administer a single antiemetic regardless of risk burden
Maintain deep neuromuscular blockade through extubation
questions.explanation: High-PONV-risk patients benefit from multimodal prophylaxis with agents from different classes and from reducing emetogenic exposure, such as limiting volatile agents and opioids when feasible. Waiting until vomiting occurs, increasing volatile near closure, or relying on a single antiemetic leaves high-risk patients undertreated.

questions.stem: A high-risk patient has received dexamethasone and ondansetron rather than relying on one antiemetic. Why is this strategy preferred?
options: Each drug lowers the other's dose
Dual therapy removes opioid nausea risk
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone and ondansetron act through different mechanisms, a steroid effect and 5-HT3 blockade, so combining them gives more protection in high-risk patients than either alone. The combination does not shorten emergence or eliminate PONV risk.

questions.stem: Near closure, surgical stimulation has fallen substantially but the patient remains deeply anesthetized. What is the most appropriate general strategy?
options: Stop all anesthesia now despite residual paralysis
Keep maximal surgical depth until the dressing is on
Increase depth because stimulation has decreased
Titrate depth down while staying adequate
questions.explanation: As stimulation falls near closure, anesthetic depth is gradually reduced so the patient emerges promptly after the last stimulus, while staying deep enough to prevent awareness and movement. Stopping abruptly with residual paralysis risks awareness, and staying maximally deep delays emergence.

questions.stem: The volatile anesthetic is turned off early while quantitative TOF still shows profound blockade and closure continues. Why is this unsafe?
options: Hypnosis may fade while paralysis hides movement
Early discontinuation ensures a faster extubation
Paralytics provide hypnosis once volatile stops
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular blockade abolishes movement but provides no hypnosis or amnesia. If the volatile agent is turned off while a deep block remains and closure continues, the patient can become aware without being able to move, so depth is maintained until neuromuscular recovery is under way.

questions.stem: For an adult with aspiration risk and a previously difficult airway, which emergence endpoint is generally safest before planned extubation?
options: Deep extubation to suppress all coughing
questions.explanation: With aspiration risk or a known difficult airway, extubation waits until the patient is fully awake, breathing adequately, and has protective reflexes, because losing the airway would be hard to rescue. Deep extubation leaves the airway unprotected, stage II carries laryngospasm risk, and residual blockade weakens the pharynx.

questions.stem: A patient has TOFR 0.95 but remains unresponsive, hypoventilatory, and unable to maintain upper-airway patency. What should be done?
options: Extubate, since a TOFR above 0.9 confirms readiness
Give sugammadex to finish reversal, then extubate
Keep intubated until awake and breathing adequately
Extubate and place a nasal airway for patency
questions.explanation: A TOF ratio of 0.95 shows neuromuscular recovery, but extubation also requires consciousness, adequate spontaneous ventilation, and the ability to keep the airway open. More sugammadex adds nothing once the ratio exceeds 0.9, and a nasal airway does not protect an unresponsive patient. Causes such as residual opioid, hypothermia, or metabolic problems are assessed.

questions.stem: Which THREE respiratory findings support extubation readiness? (Select 3)
options: Acceptable oxygenation on an appropriate FiO2
Sustained ventilation without significant apnea or obstruction
questions.explanation: Respiratory readiness for extubation includes adequate spontaneous tidal volumes and minute ventilation, acceptable oxygenation on a modest FiO2, and sustained breathing without apnea or obstruction. A TOF ratio below 0.9, persistent hypercapnia from opioids, or dependence on controlled ventilation means the patient is not ready.

questions.stem: Which THREE neurologic or airway-protective findings support awake extubation readiness? (Select 3)
options: Effective cough or gag/handling of secretions
Coughing while still in stage II
Purposeful response to command when appropriate
questions.explanation: For awake extubation, the patient should follow commands purposefully, cough or swallow effectively, and keep the upper airway open. Eye opening without command following and coughing during stage II can occur while reflexes are hyperactive and unreliable, and adequate tidal volume alone does not show airway protection.

questions.stem: Neostigmine is given when the TOF count is 1 of 4, and 20 minutes later the TOF ratio is still well below 0.9. What best explains the poor reversal?
options: The neostigmine dose was given too slowly
Rocuronium cannot be reversed by neostigmine
Neostigmine has a ceiling effect in deep block
questions.explanation: Neostigmine works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, and once the enzyme is fully inhibited, more drug adds nothing, so it cannot overcome a deep block; reversal is unreliable until at least 2 to 4 twitches have returned. Sugammadex reverses deeper rocuronium block. Glycopyrrolate only blocks muscarinic side effects.

questions.stem: A patient already has a quantitative TOF ratio of 1.0 when a full dose of neostigmine is given. What is a recognized risk?
questions.explanation: When the block has fully recovered, a full neostigmine dose can cause excess acetylcholine at the junction, producing a depolarizing-type weakness of upper airway and other muscles, so neostigmine is reduced or omitted when the TOF ratio is already 0.9 or higher. It does not trigger MH or cause sedation.

questions.stem: A patient is awake with TOFR 0.95 and adequate ventilation, but marked upper-airway edema is suspected. Why should extubation still be delayed or modified?
options: Awake patients clear edema on their own
Edema matters only after PACU arrival
questions.explanation: Airway edema is a mechanical narrowing that neuromuscular recovery and wakefulness do not fix, so an awake, fully reversed patient can still obstruct after extubation; a cuff leak test, steroids, an exchange catheter, or delayed extubation may be used. Edema can cause obstruction immediately.

questions.stem: A patient with a known difficult airway is otherwise ready for extubation. What must be established before the ETT is removed?
options: A normal BIS value before removing the tube
A rescue plan with equipment and help on hand
A normal blood pressure before extubation
questions.explanation: Extubating a known difficult airway requires an explicit plan for reintubation, the equipment for it, such as a videolaryngoscope and exchange catheter, and skilled help present. BIS and blood pressure do not address airway rescue, and deep extubation removes control of a difficult airway.

questions.stem: After prolonged neck surgery, which finding most directly supports concern for laryngeal/upper-airway edema before extubation?
options: Swelling with little or no cuff leak
questions.explanation: After prolonged neck surgery, visible swelling with an absent or minimal leak around the deflated cuff raises concern for laryngeal or upper-airway edema, although the cuff-leak test is not definitive. Vasopressor needs, emergence tachycardia, and neuromuscular recovery do not predict airway edema.

questions.stem: After extubation following prolonged neck surgery, inspiratory stridor develops while SpO2 is 93% and the patient is alert. Which treatment is most appropriate first?
options: Immediate reintubation with a large tube
questions.explanation: Postextubation stridor from laryngeal edema in an alert, oxygenating patient is treated first with nebulized racemic epinephrine, along with humidified oxygen, head elevation, and steroids. Reintubation is for failure and a large tube worsens edema, steroids act over hours, and albuterol treats lower airway bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A 3-hour colectomy is still in the maintenance phase with an hour of surgery remaining. When should the anesthesia provider begin planning drug offset, reversal, analgesia, and extubation strategy?
questions.explanation: Emergence planning begins during maintenance, about an hour before the end here, so long-acting opioids, reversal, antiemetics, and the extubation strategy are timed to work when surgery ends. Waiting until the last suture leaves drugs peaking at the wrong time and delays a smooth wake-up.

questions.stem: Which THREE risks should shape the extubation plan before emergence begins? (Select 3)
options: Need to raise volatile at emergence
questions.explanation: Before emergence the provider anticipates airway edema, a difficult reintubation if the airway is lost, and aspiration risk, along with OSA and possible postoperative ventilation, so equipment and personnel match the risk. More blocker or more volatile works against emergence, and reversal agents do not cause hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A patient with OSA, BMI 41, difficult mask ventilation, and prior difficult intubation is nearing emergence. Which extubation strategy is most appropriate?
options: Extubate when SpO2 alone is normal
Extubate deep, then place an LMA
questions.explanation: OSA, severe obesity, and prior difficulty with mask ventilation and intubation make loss of the airway after extubation dangerous, so the patient is extubated fully awake, semi-upright, with reintubation equipment and help ready. Deep techniques, including deep extubation to an LMA, remove airway control in a patient who is hard to rescue.

questions.stem: A high-PONV-risk patient also has residual neuromuscular blockade. Which THREE medication priorities belong in emergence planning? (Select 3)
options: A single antiemetic regardless of score
Antiemetics based on her Apfel score
questions.explanation: With residual blockade and high PONV risk, emergence medications include appropriate neuromuscular reversal, antiemetics matched to the Apfel score, and analgesics titrated to breathing. Deep extubation is unsafe with residual weakness, flumazenil does not reverse neuromuscular block, and one agent is not enough for high risk.

questions.stem: Near emergence, end-tidal sevoflurane falls to roughly 0.3Ã¢ÂÂ0.4 age-adjusted MAC and the patient begins responding to commands. Which MAC concept does this transition approximate?
questions.explanation: MAC-awake, about 0.3 to 0.4 MAC, is the end-tidal concentration at which patients begin to respond to commands during emergence. It is well below the 1.0 MAC that prevents movement and the roughly 1.5 MAC that blunts adrenergic responses (MAC-BAR).

questions.stem: The patient is bucking on the ETT but does not yet meet extubation criteria. Which FOUR small-dose medications may blunt coughing while emergence continues? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Small doses of IV lidocaine, an opioid, dexmedetomidine, or propofol blunt airway reflexes and coughing on the tube while the patient continues toward extubation criteria. Neostigmine reverses blockade and does not suppress cough, and rocuronium would undo the recovery.

questions.stem: In PACU after rocuronium, the patient has shallow respirations and weak grip; quantitative TOFR is 0.68. Which diagnosis best explains the pattern?
options: Isolated opioid effect despite the low TOFR
questions.explanation: Shallow breathing and weak grip with a quantitative TOF ratio of 0.68 mean residual neuromuscular blockade, which weakens the diaphragm and pharyngeal muscles and raises the risk of aspiration and reintubation. Opioids cause slow breathing without weakness, and the low ratio rules out adequate recovery.

questions.stem: Which TWO complications are increased by residual neuromuscular weakness after extubation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Residual neuromuscular blockade weakens the diaphragm and pharyngeal muscles, impairing ventilation, airway patency, cough, and swallowing, which leads to respiratory distress, aspiration, and reintubation. Urinary retention, delirium, nausea, and hypothermia have other causes.

questions.stem: TOFR is 0.7 with weak ventilation after surgery. Which THREE interventions address residual neuromuscular blockade? (Select 3)
options: Provide additional reversal when appropriate for the blocker, depth, and prior reversal given
Rely on a sustained 5-second head lift
Extubate now since the patient is awake
Allow additional time for spontaneous recovery with ventilatory support
Repeat high-dose neostigmine regardless of depth
questions.explanation: A TOF ratio of 0.7 with weak breathing calls for continued ventilatory support, quantitative monitoring, time, and reversal suited to the blocker and depth, such as sugammadex after rocuronium. Wakefulness and a head lift are insensitive to residual block, and repeated neostigmine has a ceiling effect.

questions.stem: Immediately after extubation, high-pitched inspiratory noise progresses to forceful respiratory effort with no airflow. Which complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: High-pitched inspiratory noise after extubation that progresses to forceful effort without airflow is laryngospasm, reflex closure of the vocal cords triggered by secretions, blood, or stimulation at a light plane. Bronchospasm causes expiratory wheeze with airflow, tongue obstruction responds to jaw thrust, and tracheomalacia is a structural problem.

questions.stem: After extubation, the chest and abdomen rock paradoxically with forceful effort but there is no audible airflow. Which finding does this most strongly indicate?
questions.explanation: Paradoxical rocking of the chest and abdomen with forceful effort but no airflow means the glottis is completely closed, so this is complete laryngospasm, a more urgent situation than partial spasm with stridor. Immediate CPAP with 100% oxygen and jaw thrust, then propofol or succinylcholine if needed, are required.

questions.stem: Postextubation stridor progresses toward absent airflow, and blood/secretions are visible at the laryngeal inlet. What should occur first while 100% oxygen and airway maneuvers are initiated?
options: Suction to remove the provoking stimulus
questions.explanation: Blood and secretions at the laryngeal inlet trigger the spasm, so prompt suctioning removes the stimulus while 100% oxygen, CPAP, and jaw thrust are applied. Succinylcholine or reintubation may follow if spasm persists, and racemic epinephrine treats edema rather than reflex closure.

questions.stem: Complete laryngospasm persists despite jaw thrust and positive pressure. Firm bilateral pressure is applied behind the mandibular ramus near the mastoid while the jaw is displaced. Which maneuver is being used?
questions.explanation: The Larson maneuver applies firm inward pressure at the laryngospasm notch, behind the ascending ramus and in front of the mastoid, while lifting the jaw. The stimulus is thought to help relax the cords. Cricoid pressure and the Sellick maneuver compress the esophagus, and BURP improves the laryngoscopic view.

questions.stem: Complete laryngospasm persists despite removing stimulation, 100% O2, positive pressure, jaw/Larson maneuvers, and rapidly worsening hypoxemia. Which drug is appropriate to break the spasm?
questions.explanation: When laryngospasm persists despite removing the stimulus, 100% oxygen, CPAP, and jaw and Larson maneuvers, with worsening hypoxemia, a small dose of succinylcholine, about 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg IV, relaxes the cords. Lidocaine may help prevent spasm but will not break it, albuterol treats bronchospasm, and atropine treats bradycardia.

questions.stem: Sugammadex has already been administered and severe laryngospasm now requires paralysis for rescue. Why may rocuronium require special consideration in this setting?
questions.explanation: Sugammadex remaining in the circulation can encapsulate rocuronium given soon afterward, so a standard dose may not produce paralysis; succinylcholine or a benzylisoquinolinium blocker is used instead. Sugammadex does not affect succinylcholine, and recurarization is not the issue here.
